body.text: The Federal Republic of Germany, it seems, has entered uncharted territory. Only once before has its dominant postwar political force, the Christian Democratic Union, won less than 10 per cent of the vote at a national or state election. That happened seventy-five years ago in the small city state of Bremen, when the party managed only 9 per cent. But the Christian Democrats beat that negative record comfortably last Sunday in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

Worse still, the party failed to reach the 5 per cent needed to sit in parliament. A whopping 33.6 point gap separated the Christian Democrats — the same party that has provided six of the Federal Republic’s ten postwar chancellors, including Konrad Adenauer (1949–1963), Helmut Kohl (1982–1998) and Angela Merkel (2005–2021) — from the party that won the most votes, the far-right Alternative for Germany, or AfD.

Two weeks earlier, the AfD had caused a similar jolt by coming first in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Having won thirty-nine out of eighty-three seats in that state’s parliament, and with the Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht (which won five seats) signalling its willingness to cut a deal, the far right is poised to form government there. It would be a first in the history of the Federal Republic.

These shocks weren’t just felt in Germany. Although the two states combined account for less than a twentieth of Germany’s population, the AfD’s unprecedented gains are eerily reminiscent of the meteoric rise of another far-right party almost a century ago. In November 1932, at the last free elections in Weimar Germany, Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ Party won 33.1 per cent of the national vote. Less than three months later, German president Paul von Hindenburg appointed a minority government with Hitler as chancellor.

That’s why the anxieties triggered outside Germany by the vote in Saxony-Anhalt surpass concerns about the vulnerability of democracy in Croatia, Finland, Czechia and Slovakia, where parties on the extreme right of the political spectrum are already part of national governing coalitions, or in Italy, which has been led for almost four years by a former member of the neo-fascist Movimento Sociale Italiano.

Is this focus on the far right’s successes in Germany justified? Yes and no. Germany is still the powerhouse of Europe, so an AfD-led federal government would have a dramatic impact on the rest of the continent. But that’s assuming the AfD’s trajectory will soon give it control of the levers of national government.

Germany’s notorious history doesn’t make it more vulnerable to the far right than, say, Britain. French voters seem more likely to elect Marine Le Pen of the far-right Rassemblement National next year than German voters are to opt for a federal government led by the AfD’s Alice Weidel at the next scheduled elections in 2029.

In fact, the German far right has for many years been kept in check, unlike rightwing extremists in Austria, Poland, France and other neighbouring countries — and that might well have been because of, rather than in spite of, Germany’s historical record. The Federal Republic’s institutions have long been attuned to the dangers of authoritarianism. Its governments have invested heavily in civic education and initiatives that promote democracy and diversity and encourage political participation, recent budget cuts by the Merz government notwithstanding.

Besides, the Constitution allows German democracy to defend itself against its enemies. Germany’s High Court, the Bundesverfassungsgericht, could declare that somebody who abuses the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution forfeits those rights, according to Article 18. “All Germans shall have the right to resist any person seeking to abolish this constitutional order if no other remedy is available,” says Article 20 (4). “Parties that, by reason of their aims or the behaviour of their adherents, seek to undermine or abolish the free democratic basic order or to endanger the existence of the Federal Republic of Germany shall be unconstitutional,” adds Article 21 (2).
So, are claims that the 2020s resemble the early 1930s simply scaremongering? Do they reflect a morbid fascination with that era rather than close attention to the present?

True, the economic circumstances in the 1930s could not have been more different from today’s. Although Germany’s economy has performed poorly in recent years (last year’s growth rate was lower than in any other OECD country), unemployment is still comparatively low and people who lose their jobs receive welfare support. In the early 1930s, Germany was in the midst of a severe economic crisis, with more than six million people unemployed by February 1932. Unemployment benefits were reduced or, for married women and youths, cut altogether.

Once Hitler was appointed to lead the German government, the Nazis could also rely on half a million paramilitary SA stromtroopers. The opposition was deeply divided; communists and Social Democrats were often keener to attack each other than fight the Nazis. A significant proportion of the conservative elite, while not necessarily in favour of a fascist takeover, had never warmed to the republic and longed for a restoration of the monarchy or some kind of authoritarian rule. Germany’s defeat in the first world war and the terms of the Treaty of Versailles had fostered deep resentments and a nationalist fervour that favoured the Nazis.

But that doesn’t mean there aren’t any parallels between the early 1930s and the mid 2020s. To recognise them, it’s useful to consider the Weimar years, and the decisions made then by political figures, without the benefit of hindsight. The conservatives in particular underestimated the Nazis’ ruthlessness and imagined Hitler’s room to manoeuvre could be easily curtailed. They believed him when he assured them he would respect the rule of law, and they didn’t take Nazi rhetoric seriously. They expected Hitler and his henchmen, who lacked the experience of governing, to fail and hence disappoint their followers.

One of the lessons of the early 1930s is that it is important to isolate the far right. That’s where the Brandmauer (firewall) comes in. Germany’s democratic parties, including the Christian Democrats and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, have vowed never to form a government that relies on AfD support. The Brandmauer is also meant to prevent any of the AfD’s legislative initiatives from succeeding: all other parties have agreed to oppose them as a matter of principle.

The Brandmauer has failed to stop the rise of the AfD, say several senior Christian Democrats. It no longer works where the AfD represents a very large proportion of the population, they argue, because it only serves to alienate AfD voters even further. And they point to the third tier of government: the many town councils and district assemblies in East Germany where the AfD is treated much like any other party.

This is not yet a position shared by Christian Democrats leader and German chancellor Friedrich Merz; and nor, it appears, is it shared by the fifteen Christian Democrats elected to sit in Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament. The prominent Christian Democrat most likely to favour collaboration with the AfD, Jens Spahn, was recently forced to resign as leader of the national parliamentary party because he and his husband paid an American woman to bear their child despite his having vehemently opposed moves to legalise surrogacy in Germany.

But the critics of the Brandmauer strategy are correct in saying that it hasn’t worked. The reason is simple: it hasn’t been applied consistently. In January last year, Merz, still in opposition, tabled a parliamentary resolution demanding that anybody attempting to “illegally” enter Germany be pushed back and that all people required to leave the country be imprisoned. The resolution only succeeded because the AfD supported it, making a mockery of Merz’s claim that the Brandmauer would hold under his leadership and the AfD’s share of the vote would be halved.

Trying to entice former Christian Democrat supporters back into the fold, Merz also adopted the AfD’s anti-migrant rhetoric on other occasions. He was not the only one who parrotted the AfD’s demands and used their vocabulary; Olaf Scholz, who led the “traffic light coalition” of Social Democrats, Greens and Free Democrats, was another, though not as blatantly as Merz. Thus politicians of centre-right and centre-left parties normalised some of the AfD’s rhetoric and thereby added to the Brandmauer’s growing porousness.

By making some of the AfD’s policies appear legitimate, Merz, Scholz and others helped to shift the entire political discourse to the right and made the AfD stronger. The northern state of Schleswig-Holstein shows how the opposite approach could have been far more successful. There, in 2017, the liberal Christian Democrat premier Daniel Günther decided to isolate the AfD after it entered state parliament for the first time. Unlike Merz and Scholz, he was uncompromising. The result: at the 2022 elections, his party’s vote increased by 11.4 percentage points and the AfD failed to reach the 5 per cent threshold. Since then, Schleswig-Holstein has been the only German state in which the AfD is not represented in parliament.

Justus Bender, a journalist with the conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung, recently published a fascinating book in which he imagined how a Spahn-led Christian Democratic Union might agree to enter a coalition with the AfD, winner of the 2033 federal election. By this circuitous route, Spahn and his colleagues want to prove the AfD isn’t fit to govern — much like conservatives in Weimar Germany wanted to demonstrate the Nazis’ incompetence when they offered Hitler the chancellorship.

Bender shows how the AfD would be able to use its position in government to begin dismantling German democracy. Much as the Nazis set about creating a one-party dictatorship in early 1933 without any resistance from their coalition partners, in 2033 the AfD’s Alice Weidel uses Spahn and his Christian Democrats to introduce a constitutional provision for binding referendums. Once she no longer needs them, she leads a minority government that bypasses parliament with the help of referendums (à la Viktor Orbán) and rules by decree (à la Donald Trump).

But is the AfD really that dangerous? Is it the twenty-first century version of Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist German Workers’ Party? Unsurprisingly, AfD leader Alice Weidel denies this, but with an astonishing argument. In January 2025, she told Elon Musk in an interview that Hitler was a “communist” and an “antisemitic socialist.” Earlier this week, she repeated this claim, saying Hitler pursued leftwing policies and was “a leftwing radical, a leftwing extremist.”

This absurd reinterpretation of the past is no laughing matter. Its aim could be to distance the AfD from historical National Socialism while reclaiming fascism as a concept. If Hitler wasn’t a fascist, so the argument might go, then the term shouldn’t be considered an insult when it’s applied to an AfD politician.

This potential reframing aside, the AfD has a point when it distinguishes its own positions from those of the Nazi party. Unlike the Sozialistische Reichspartei, a small far-right party that was moderately successful in the early 1950s and was banned by the Bundesverfassungsgericht in 1952, the AfD is not a neo-Nazi party in the same way the Movimento Sociale Italiano was a neo-fascist party. The Sozialistische Reichspartei considered itself a successor of the National Socialist German Workers’ Party. It used the latter’s program as a blueprint for its own policy positions and denied the Holocaust had ever happened.

The AfD doesn’t do any of that. In fact, as I observed in an Inside Story essay a few years back, one of the AfD’s heroes is Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg, the army officer who tried to assassinate Hitler on 20 July 1944. Notwithstanding the deliberate provocations by some of its leaders that evoke the Nazis, the AfD is more closely associated with the New Right than with traditional far-right reactionaries. Björn Höcke and other AfD heavyweights reference representatives of the so-called Conservative Revolution, an ultraconservative movement active between 1918 and 1933, most of whom were not Nazis themselves but inspired the Nazis.

Attempts to demonstrate the AfD’s affinity with Hitler’s party detract attention from the two main reasons why it ought to be considered dangerous: because of its commitment to an exclusive, ethnically defined nationalism, and because it rejects liberal democracy.

The party’s ethnonationalist agenda leads prominent AfD figures to call for the “remigration” of people who are not German by descent and for selectively withholding the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution from non-citizens and citizens with a migrant background. Their rejection of key tenets of liberal democracy is evident in their disdain for democratic deliberation and informed debate and their demonisation of the political establishment.

How radical is the AfD? Ask Marine Le Pen of the Rassemblement National or Geert Wilders of the Dutch Partij voor de Vrijheid. Like other representatives of European far-right parties, they don’t want the AfD to join their political group in the European parliament because they fear the AfD’s extremism could taint their own reputations.

Or listen to AfD leader Alice Weidel speaking in the German parliament. On 9 September, she accused Merz of “driving Germany towards national bankruptcy,” while “deindustrialisation is sweeping across our country with gathering momentum.” The “consequences of mass migration” supposedly include “the hatred foreign groups harbour toward what is our own… hatred toward Christians… hatred toward Germans… hatred toward Germany.” “And on top of that,” she told Merz, “you pay them.”

Other AfD politicians seem more moderate: Ulrich Siegmund, for example, the congenial leader of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and former spruiker of household fragrances. But turn to the manifesto published by the AfD’s branch in Saxony-Anhalt ahead of the 2026 elections and you’ll find a few gems: The “authorities treat foreigners with laxity and leniency, while taking ruthless action against their own citizens who hold dissenting views,” it reads. An AfD-led government “will primarily support art that contributes to the shaping of German identity.”

The manifesto is particularly detailed when it comes to education (which is the responsibility of states). Support for schools with a commitment to anti-racism would be terminated because “Under the guise of wanting to combat racism, action is being taken against legitimate right-wing and patriotic views.” “For humanitarian reasons,” the AfD is not averse to providing schooling to the children of refugees. But “this should take place in separate classes… to convey the message to refugee children that their stay in Germany is merely temporary… [and] to shield our own children from the various stresses that arise from shared instruction with children from completely different cultures.”

When asked a few days after the election about an Israeli arms manufacturer interested in establishing a plant in Saxony-Anhalt, Siegmund said that he was not against the production of military equipment in principle, “as the necessary tools will be needed for the subsequent remigration and deportation offensive.” Sometime in October he will probably be sworn in as state premier of Saxony-Anhalt. His government will waste no time in implementing as much of the AfD’s program as possible. Those who tell themselves that things won’t turn out that badly and doubt comparisons with the Nazi party’s grab for power might have a rude awakening.

A third state election was held in Germany this month, in Berlin. Althought its population is roughly the same as those of the two other states where people went to the polls, combined, outside Germany the election in the nation’s capital received less attention. That’s because the AfD came third (though it did increase its share of the vote) behind the left-wing Linke on 25.7 per cent and the Christian Democrats on 18.8 per cent. As in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the three left and centre-left parties should be able to govern together, although a Christian Democrat–led government, with the Greens and the Social Democrats as minor partners, is also possible.

During much of Berlin’s election campaign, I stayed in Wedding, a lively but comparatively poor suburb in the inner north with a high proportion of first- and second-generation migrants. One in three residents is a non-citizen. The AfD performed poorly but the Linke was particularly strong, attracting more than half of the vote in some areas, as if to demonstrate that racism and calls for “remigration” are less appealing where ethnic and cultural diversity are most pronounced.

Across the road from my hotel was a park with an eleven-metre high monument. Called Trümmersäule (literally: “rubble column”), its four sides are labelled “slavery,” “destruction,” “reconstruction” (Aufbau) and “democracy.” Gerhard Schultze-Seehof, the artist who created the column in 1954, used tiles, bricks and other wartime rubble to tell stories featuring figures reminiscent of those of Keith Haring murals.

As far as I could tell, passers-by were paying no attention to the column and its stories, as if to confirm Robert Musil’s observation that monuments “are impregnated with something that repels attention, causing the glance to roll right off, like water droplets off an oilcloth.”

The monument was commissioned to celebrate the rebuilding of (West) Berlin after the war: the reconstruction of its infrastructure, housing stock and social fabric. It juxtaposes “slavery” — the scenes depicted on the column could be read as a reference both to Nazi rule between 1933 and 1945 and to Stalinist repression after the war — and the results of the Allied bombing campaign, on the one hand, and depictions of the postwar recovery, on the other. Aufbau, the term used by Schultze-Seehof, didn’t necessarily only mean the re-building of Berlin. The sides depicting Aufbau and Demokratie could be read as depictions of the present and the future.

The side representing democracy shows people who are busy: they are engaged in animated conversation and support one another. The images convey the sense of a well-functioning community. It is the kind of harmonious community nostalgically imagined by many supporters of the AfD, which claims the present is terrible and the future bleak — unless the current “system” is swept away, that is, in which case the future would look like the 1950s (or at least like the 1950s as they are now imagined).

The government’s promise is not entirely different. We are going through a difficult patch, Merz and his colleagues concede, but we are on the mend, and once the necessary reforms have been implemented Germany will be fine again. And when the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine eventually end, things will be as they were before — maybe not like the 1950s, but perhaps like the decade just before the 2008 financial crisis.

That’s an illusion, of course. Endless progress, with democracy’s role merely to distribute an ever-growing surplus (rather than to redistribute existing wealth), is no longer sustainable. Somebody ought to tell Germans. The current government seems unable to do that. It’s also unable to convey a positive vision in which some things will need to be dismantled to make the world liveable for all.

The park with the monument is named after Max Josef Metzger. He was a Catholic priest and peace activist who was tried by the Nazis’ Volksgerichtshof (People’s Court) in 1943 for drafting a “Democratic Manifesto,” sentenced to death and executed on 17 April 1944. In his manifesto, he imagined a new Germany in which social justice was paramount within a broader “United States of Europe.” Metzger’s text could serve as a reminder of the second truth Germans ought to be told: that the modern nation-state is an anachronism, that national governments are no longer able to shape their countries’ destinies, and that claims to seal off borders or to deport all migrants are feeble attempts to disguise that impotence.

The Trümmersäule’s stark contrast between destruction and reconstruction, slavery and democracy suggests that a clean break with the past had occurred. It had not. The yearning for the innocent 1950s likewise imagines an innocence that never existed — least of all in the 1950s.

Two days before the Trümmersäule was unveiled on Sunday, 20 June 1954, the West German parliament passed an amnesty law with the support of a majority of the opposition. It allowed those who could claim they had acted in pursuit of an official duty during the war or claim they had carried out an order were no longer tried if the expected sentence didn’t exceed three years in prison. The 400,000 Germans who benefited from the law included Nazis who had assumed false identities in order evade Allied prosecution.

That same Sunday, West German hopes of doing well at the Football World Cup in Switzerland seemed extinguished when Sepp Herberger’s team was beaten by Hungary by a five-goal margin. That was not the end of the story, though. Two weeks later, West Germany would surprise the world by winning the Cup, beating Hungary three goals to two in the final. The so-called miracle of Berne was later identified as the launching pad for West Germany’s economic miracle; Helmut Rahn’s goal a few minutes before full-time turned out to be one of the most momentous events of the 1950s.

The links between Germany’s fortunes and those of its national side are often underrated. Take the 2014 World Cup — would the generosity on display a year later when Angela Merkel decided not to close Germany’s borders otherwise have lasted as long as it did? And surely the extreme disgruntlement that fuelled the AfD’s victories this month would have been less pronounced if the German team’s embarrassing performance this summer hadn’t — once again — led to a premature exit from the world cup.

At last, there is reason for hope. On 15 August, Jürgen “Kloppo” Klopp took over as coach of the German side. Everyone knows he should have been appointed years ago, but then he was busy winning Premier League and Champions League silverware with Liverpool. “Jürgen said to me, you know./ We’ll win the Premier League, you know./ He said so./ I’m in love with him and I feel fine,” Liverpool’s fans used to sing.

The contrast between a chancellor lacking empathy and unable to convey a positive vision and a football coach whose ability to touch his audience is perhaps unrivalled has not gone unnoticed. The “positive patriotism” that “Kloppo” wants to reawaken makes me cringe, but the prospect of a far-right party on the rampage is enough to convince me his talents are what’s needed now.

Let people love him, and let them feel fine. And then get him to explain to them that we must stay well clear of anything that resembles the 1950s; that a bit of flag-waving is okay, but nationalism is poisonous; that the modern nation-state is an anachronistic relic from an era well before the 1950s; and that old-style progress is no longer warranted as long as we are moving towards justice and sustainability. •
